name: Pirc: Austrian Attack
summary: The Austrian Attack (1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4) is White's sharpest anti-Pirc, building an e4-d4-f4 centre for e5 and a kingside pawn storm.
intro: The Austrian Attack is White's most ambitious response to the Pirc Defence, arising after 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3 O-O. With the thrust 4.f4 White stakes out a huge pawn centre on e4, d4, and f4, refusing to let Black's hypermodern setup off the hook. The idea is direct and aggressive: prepare the e5 advance to gain space and drive back Black's knight, and then throw the kingside pawns forward with a later f5 or h4-h5 to open lines against the fianchettoed king. Black, for his part, welcomes the challenge, because such an extended centre can be undermined with the freeing breaks ...c5 and ...e5. The result is one of the sharpest theoretical battlegrounds in the entire Pirc complex.
line: e4 d6 d4 Nf6 Nc3 g6 f4 Bg7 Nf3 O-O

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Austrian Attack is a race between White's central expansion and Black's counterattack against it. White's pawns on e4, d4, and f4 grant a commanding space advantage, and the natural plan is to complete development with Bd3 or Be2, castle short, and then advance in the centre or on the kingside. If White is allowed to play e5 under good circumstances, followed by a pawn storm with f5, h4, and h5, Black's king can come under a ferocious attack. The g7-bishop and the half-open lines that appear after the pawns clash give the position its combative, double-edged flavour.

Black's counterplay is built around the two thematic pawn breaks. The move ...c5 strikes at the base of White's centre and, after an exchange on c5 or d4, opens the c-file and activates the g7-bishop along the long diagonal. The alternative ...e5 hits d4 head-on and, if White captures, can leave the centre fluid and the e4-pawn exposed. Black typically completes development with ...Nc6 or ...Na6, ...Bg4 to pressure d4 and f3, and sometimes ...Qb6 to add to the pressure. Whether White's big centre becomes a crushing spearhead or an overextended target is the central strategic question of the line.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The principal main line runs 6.Bd3, developing the bishop to its most active diagonal before castling. Black replies with either 6...Nc6, immediately pressuring d4 and preparing ...e5, or 6...Na6 followed by ...c5, hitting the centre from the flank. After 6...Nc6 7.e5 the sharpest positions arise, with Black continuing 7...dxe5 8.fxe5 and then ...Nd5 or ...Nd7 to blockade and counterattack. The lines with ...c5 are equally critical, since after 6.Bd3 the break can lead to fast piece play against White's centre. The quieter 6.Be2 keeps the bishop more modest but supports the same central and kingside ambitions.

White can also strike at once with 6.e5, the most forcing try, when 6...Nfd7 7.h4 launches an immediate kingside pawn storm and produces the wildest positions of the whole variation. Play may continue with ...c5 and ...Nc6, and both sides race to open lines against the enemy king. Alternatively White develops calmly and delays e5, aiming to keep the tension until the pieces are ideally placed. Because the pawn structure can transform so quickly, precise move orders matter enormously here, and long forcing sequences have been analysed deeply by theory.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Pirc Defence takes its name from the Slovenian grandmaster Vasja Pirc, who championed the ...d6 and ...g6 setup in the 1930s and 1940s as a flexible, counterattacking answer to 1.e4; the line is also historically associated with Anatoly Ufimtsev, and is sometimes called the Pirc-Ufimtsev. The defence embodies the hypermodern idea of conceding the centre in order to strike back at it, and it grew into a respected mainstream opening in the second half of the twentieth century.

Against this counterattacking scheme, the Austrian Attack with 4.f4 emerged as White's most aggressive antidote, seeking to punish Black's slow development by seizing maximum space and attacking directly. It became a favourite of ambitious 1.e4 players looking to avoid a slow positional grind, and it remains the critical test of the Pirc at every level. Its combination of a broad pawn centre and rapid kingside expansion continues to attract those who want to meet the Pirc with immediate, uncompromising aggression.
